I used to be a smoker, and one time I was having some difficulty looking for a new apartment because so many of the listings I encountered stipulated "no smokers". My brother encouraged me not to worry about it because you could always consider any gaps between smoking as having temporarily quit. If I quit smoking in the morning, only to start smoking again that afternoon, how could they prove that I was always a smoker, and not just the victim of a failed quitting attempt. As a disclaimer, I'd like to mention that I'd never smoke inside a rented apartment. My point is that there's some ambiguity between "pause" as an "end".

When most relationships talk about witholding sex, they usually mean "last Saturday" or "for the past few weeks", not "for the rest of our lives". It's a gap, not an end. If a relationship truly turns asexual, particularly if that decision is one-sided, then that very will could justify the end of a relationship, but most would be wary to end a relationship based only on a temporary rift.

Whether or not ending a relationship over the witholding of sex is justified is less important than whether or not it is practical. Breaking up is often incredibly unpleasant for everyone involved, and choosing whether to exit a relationship is a serious decision that's not to be taken lightly. If a relationship shows no signs of ever resulting in sex again, then it's probably worth going through the emotional and logistical turmoil that a breakup usually entails. Conversely, if sex was denied on Monday, few would be willing to throw the relationship away by Tuesday.

Really, this all comes down to conflict resolution. Witholding sex is a mean thing to do, especially if done deliberately out of spite, but it's just one of the thousands of ways that couples can choose to hurt eachother. You can no more justify witholding sex than implementing the silent treatment, using excessive sarcasm, holding a grudge, or any of the other sorts of disfunction that couples can sometimes fall into when engaged in an altercation, but, while unpleasant, very few of these sorts of behavior warrant an immediate and unconditional breakup. The truth is, it takes time to learn to be in a relationship, and most couples will encounter some of these sorts of hostility from time to time as they learn to resolve their disagreements more responsibly/respectfully.

So, while I'd agree that witholding sex is destructive, and can't usually be justified as part of a healthy part of a relationship, I'd disagree that witholding sex immediately represents or warrants an end of the relationship.
